text: This new burger joint just opened. Generally, new restaurants try to open with a big bang. Staff and management are plenty and they are usually full of enthusiasm, focused on customer service and running around just making sure that everything is going as well as possible. For this reason we often choose to wait until the "staff calms down" before going to a newly opened restaurant. But, we were wanting a burger so we decided to just suck it up and go to Teddy's just days after opening... we were mentally prepared for the super happy employees, the over tentative managers and such. Our mental preparation for a zeal-induced staff was not needed. Burgers ranged from $8.00 - $9.50 all burgers are served with fries. If you want something other than fries, you will be charged an additional 1.00. Burgers are 1/2 pound. The size of the burger and the automatic inclusion of fries make a pretty hefty meal.... for a large man. Frankly, offering a smaller burger (maybe a 1/3 pound) or offering the burger only without fries would have suited my 5'4", 125-pound body. The nacho burger was tasty and the meat was a nice medium so it was not dry. My husbands Cajun Burger had some nice flavor but the meat was clearly over cooked and dry as an old shoe. It required multiple gulps of fluid to assure that the bites did not lodge in his airway. The fries had potential, but were mildly warm at best. Seasoned salt was poorly distributed on them, thus one bite little salt the next bite huge amount of salt. We also ordered some chips and salsa which was totally unremarkable - chips and the salsa, I suspect, can be found at the local Gordons Food Service. The environment was tragic. The choices of materials used, the total FAILURE to properly manage sound makes this environment extremely uncomfortable. As we placed our order, we could barely hear the person and she could barely hear us. The ultra industrial ceilings, the TVs blaring, and only 35 people added enough noise into the space that it was near impossible to even have a conversation. Oh! The SWEET relief when we stepped outside to walk to our car. We just sat in our car for a minute just to take a deep breath. I can only imagine what this place sounds like when it is raining outside... I suspect that the owner of this restaurant has high hopes to create several of these "joints" around the Indianapolis area and maybe even offer franchise opportunities. But, right now this place is a total miss with their own goals outlined on their website.... "The company's success will be directly linked to great customer service, generous portions of quality food, affordable pricing and an ability to create an atmosphere that is enjoyable, relaxing, clean and ultimately unforgettable." "Great customer service": If they were "working the tables", they would have known about the problems with our food (which is really shocking for a newly opened restaurant - they usually hit the tables multiple times with multiple people... but not here!) "Generous portions": Yep generous for a 200-pound man, coming in from a hard days work. "Affordable pricing": Nope "Atmosphere that is enjoyable, relaxing": Nope, nope, nope! Not even close,... it would have been more relaxing in the middle of a rodeo. "Ultimately unforgettable": yep, but not in the way that they hope. This place is lacking in a real professional touch. Its felt with the choices of materials, their selection of a very poor location and the lack of understanding of guest comfort and the failure to assure that guests are satisfied with their meal and experience.

I did think that the Eclipse bar and the Moonrise bar were both being ran by a mixologist with a subtle but loving hand. I wish I would've enjoyed the food more, but much like the other reviewers I will still return to the Moonrise but I will skip the Eclipse and make my way to the bar. text: Ever since I came across Vintage in an battered in-flight magazine, I've been dreaming of wine. Friday night, two of us stopped in for a drink. My friend pulled me past the unmanned host station (complete with sign: "Please wait to be seated"), securing a table by the bar. A crowd filled the patio and then some, making conversation and clattering silverware, a din that fit nicely with the upbeat music. (Throw in the dimly-lit interior, and you've got a good third date spot.) Vintage isn't Tria, but sometimes you don't want Tria. An impressive, steampunk wine bottle chandelier looms above the bar, a bar which stocks a surprising amount of liquor for a wine bar. (No complaints here.) Of course, there's wine: my friend enjoyed her Riesling, while I found my glass - an aromatic South African Vrede en Lust, Karien '06 ($7) - to be challenging, taking a bit of warming up to. We sampled their escargot ($11), which came with snail tongs and forks, but not a ton of flavor. Not terribly disappointing, and the butter was tasty enough. The red pepper and basil bruschetta ($6.50) was better, with a fresh crispness. When we were done, our table was cleared straightaway. Considering how busy it was, we were pleased with the service. Duane (?) and Mike were pleasant, and gave us plenty of attention. I'll be back to Vintage to try a wine flight; don't forget to check out the chalkboard specials behind the bar!

text: My poor grandmother brought my mom, grandfather and I to this place because she had a buy 1 buffet, get 1 free coupon. Why do I say poor grandmother? Because she had no idea how horribly bad this place was going to be and how much we all would complain and make fun of it! The first thing we noticed entering the buffet were ridiculous signs posted everywhere saying they had the right to charge you for uneaten food and that if you wanted the "all you can eat crab legs" (which were just single unappetizing looking legs, not clusters, as part of the buffet) it was like an extra $6 or so. Not very inviting. The next thing that was evident was the poor service. We hardly got a greeting, were lead to our seats, and then left wondering if we could get up and start the buffet. Then came the worst Chinese food I (actually all of us) ever ever had! Oh, there were plenty of selections and quantities out, however everything that I sampled was so overcooked, dry, tough and tasteless that it was just embarrassing. The soup had oil sheens on top and did not taste how it was supposed to (just gross!) The ribs had just a crusty finish to the bone (no meat), the Hunan chicken you couldn't even stick your fork through it because it was so hard, the roast beef (you cut yourself with a weapon) was dry and tasteless... I could just go on and on. We couldn't stop laughing as we questioned each other, "oh, how is that?" and we would just push our plate aside with all the food left on it shaking our heads saying DISGUSTING. The only edible things were the "doughnuts", chicken and mushrooms, and I would say the sushi which I did have a few pieces of, however they weren't labeled and because of the poor quality of everything else in the buffet, I personally questioned how fresh it really was and did not go back for seconds. Since my mom also had some sushi, I guess it was the mussels in garlic sauce that made me spend an hour in the bathroom when we got home. So now it's the end of our meal, and thank goodness they did not charge us for "uneaten food" because that's all that was left on our plates. We bypassed the hard-looking pastries for dessert and was happy to find they had an ice-cream cooler. How can they mess up ice-cream in a carton, right? Oh, but they did! So gross, they had the ice-cream scoops in this NASTY container of brown water (seriously the vision of it now is tempting me to gag) and the ice-cream had this gross water apparently frozen on top of portions of it from people using those scoops. After our check was brought to us, I had asked for another refill on my drink (which each time I needed one, it took forever and a day to get) and they finally bring me out a half-full glass of my beverage with no ice in it! REALLY?!? They didn't even get the bill right using my grandmother's coupon, but my grandparents didn't care to argue the point, they just wanted to get out of the place. As we were leaving we asked each other, "so... on a scale of 1-10, what would you rate this place?" Each of us agreed on a NEGATIVE 10. It was just really that bad!!! P.S. For the life of me I can not comprehend why there are good reviews on this place. My visit took place in late September of this year. Is it possible that I entered some alternate dimension as I walked through "Oriental Super-bad Buffet"'s doors? I wouldn't risk going back to find out. Wish Yelp would let you rate a place 0 stars.

text: I have eaten at Marathon (this location) more times than I care to admit, and I have no earthly idea why I kept coming back. I used to live and work in the neighborhood, and it is convenient, but looking back, there are SO many other convenient places that (1) serve better food, (2) have better service, or (3) both. Really, there are two Marathons here, and they each deserve a review. There is the weekday lunch Marathon and the weekday evening/weekend Marathon. It's almost as though these restaurants are the alter-ego of one another, and just happen to share space. Very strange. During the week and the lunch rush, Marathon is not a bad choice. They are crowded and rushed, but the food gets out pretty fast (and generally correctly) and the tables turn quickly. To accommodate the largest number of patrons, they do have tables packed so tightly together that you can literally hear entire conversations from nearby tables, but it can be interesting to occasionally eavesdrop and hear about someone else's dysfunctional life for a change! Weekday lunch is also when the "A-team" of servers tend to work. The service is pretty good, despite the apparent chaos throughout the restaurant (I can only imagine working the kitchen line during a weekday lunch shift), and the food is at its peak (which while generally a plus, isn't saying much here). I quickly learned to stick with basic stuff like sandwiches and soups (the Matzo ball rocks!), because salads (yes, salads) and more complicated entrees get messed up way too frequently. Then there is the evening shift. This is where things really come unglued. If the lunch shift servers are the "A-team," then this is the "D-team." Most of the servers we have had in the evenings and on weekends seem like they wound up working at Marathon because pumping gas was too complicated. In the 3 years I lived nearby and ate an occasional dinner at Marathon (apparently I am just lazy), I don't think we ever had a meal where everything was correct in our order and we enjoyed good service. More often than not, the order was wrong in at least one way (seriously, how do you mess up a Caesar salad?), or the waiter disappeared for 20 minutes, or the temperature in the restaurant was hovering just above meat locker level. Sandwiches with the wrong meat (yes, really), salads with the wrong dressing, and entirely wrong dishes were delivered with apathy and discourtesy on a routine basis. On the rare occasion that I was either particularly motivated or so pissed off that I decided to speak with a manager, the line was always the same: something about the server or kitchen staff being new/undertrained/high/mentally deficient. And yet we returned. Again and again. I think the last straw was when they were changing menus a while ago and diners at our table got different menus and the server tried to explain that neither of the menus was correct but that he would tell us what the kitchen could make that night. I love a good walking menu at a red gravy Italian joint, but at Marathon it was just too much. The good: Matzo ball soup (as good as any New York deli) The bad: EVERYTHING ELSE The ugly: see "bad, the"

text: Do you know Al Merrick? Me neither, but the hand he's had in shaping (pun intended) modern surfing is known all over the world. If Kelly Slater and Rob Machado trust him, who am I to argue? My story: an impromptu surf trip to New Zealand lands in my lap a couple of weeks ago... YESSS!! Of course, I'll NEED (yeah, right - any excuse) a new board for sure. Something shorter, for ease of travel. Something that paddles easily, and catches anything - who knows what the waves'll be like in NZ? And it's gotta be easy to ride - why would I want to spend my whole trip getting used to a new board? ...found the board that fit the bill at cisurfboards.com. The Biscuit. I didn't choose it, it chose me... Whatever. On their easily navigable website, I found a list of all the retailers that sell CI's boards, and called every shop from Australia to Honolulu to up and down the West Coast. Come to find out the Biscuit's a brand new model - no one's gonna see one 'til June. LAME! Out of desperation, I called the shop, and spoke with Kim: Alan G: Kim, I NEED a new Biscuit for my trip to NZ, and I'm leaving in like, ten days. Kim: Let me check... (pause) Hmm, it doesn't seem like we've shipped any out yet. I know we've got a whole bunch here though. Alan G: I KNOW that you haven't shipped any out yet - can you just send me one? Kim: No. We have an agreement with all our local shops not to sell direct from here. Alan G: (covering the phone) SHIT! (uncovering the phone) So, there's no way then, huh? Kim: Well, I suppose if your local shop doesn't have any Biscuits, (Didn't she just tell me that NO ONE had any?) and they didn't mind us selling you one, Scott, the shop manager, MIGHT send one to you. So after about 30 minutes of nicing-up my local shop owner, (Thanks Jeff!) I got permission, and called Scott. Alan G: Scott, I just spoke with Kim. She said I should ask you to send me a Biscuit. Scott: We don't do that. Alan G: I know, but Kim said you MIGHT make an exception if I got permission from my local seller, and told you how much I really, REALLY wanted it for my trip to NZ. Scott: Your local shop is cool with that? Alan G: Yes. Scott: What size do you want? You like Future fins or FCS? When do you need it? Alan G: 5'8". Future. NOW. Six days later, and I'm pleased as punch. Got it in the mail today!

text: I guess it comes down to food being a subjective & relative matter. After hearing about the place, I went down and tried it. I ordered the "Special Pho" (Pho is a good indicator of quality for any Vietnamese restaurant). After tasting it, I have to say it wasn't worth the visit. The flavor of the broth was bland and it didn't come with all the usual meats that would make this "Special". It was definitely below average of all the Pho I've ever tasted (and I've eaten a lot). I've actually made better at home. Additionally, we asked for tea and it turned out the tea was $2.50 for a little pot - another disappointment. My usual dining philosophy is that no Asian restaurants should ever charge for tea or white rice. Overall, with taste being relative, in Santa Barbara, Saigon is probably ok for many people. However, if they opened this restaurant in San Gabriel, Santa Ana, San Jose, or even Northridge, I don't think it would last beyond 2 days. For myself, one visit is enough. But the restaurant is clean and it seems they put effort into making the place look nice. The atmosphere is modern with plants and a cyclo for decoration. The look is tasteful. Too bad the food did not match up to the surrounding. Tip: If you really want good Vietnamese food and willing to drive a little, go to Pho Saigon in Port Hueneme. You'll get more authentic flavors there.

text: Checked this place out for the Flyers big comeback win over the Bruins last night. (Which was freaking amazing.) The place would have gotten 3-4 stars as a place to watch sports. Though, I'll agree, that horn is pretty over-the-top, loud and annoying. Also, not the worst tap selection I've seen at a sports bar. Aside from the regular domestics they did have Sam Adams lager, Sam Adams summer, Dogfish Head 90 min. (!) and Allagash White. There was a $3 Friday special which included $3 domestics and some other things. However, that's where the good ceased. Unfortunately I didn't try the much praised guava wings. It had white rice in it, which is a bit weird. She said it was bland and pretty gross. Definitely not the place to go for vegetarian fare. As everyone else said, the fries were good. Unfortunately too, for a relatively busy game night the service was substandard. There were one or two bartenders working their asses off, and we had to praise them, because as they were mixing drinks as fast as they could 1 or 2 other waiters/servers were drinking their own drinks behind the bar. Because of this, even though our tender was working hard, it slowed all of the service down. It was a bit of a mess. Managers had to step in to get drinks. The table service was non-existent (I think there was 1 server for all the tables) so people were repeatedly getting frustrated and coming directly to the bar to order drinks and food. I would consider going back for a game, just because of the things listed at the top. BUT, otherwise, not nearly the best bar in South Philly.

text: I like the nostalgic architecture / decor and convenience the Ardmore Macy's confers its guests. My friend & I planned to buy a few items for her boyfriend from the men's dept on the basement level. We also planned to shop for ourselves upstairs UNTIL a sales associate hollered at us. Yes, she LITERALLY shouted at us to say we HAD to pay for the two measly items (socks!) before leaving the dept. I don't know if she was desperate for commission. She certainly didn't serve us, so why would she earn commission? Maybe she needed receipts to show management there's activity & avoid trimming hours... but who yells at shoppers? I doubt this is taught in orientation / training. Appalled by this service, I asked if paying for items in individual depts was a new policy. She said it wasn't, but it was increasingly being enforced... I doubt it. Enforcing this policy would compromise additional revenues in other departments. By the time the sales transaction was complete, my friend & I no longer wanted to shop upstairs -- or at any another Macy's. When the associate explicitly 'apologized' for shouting at us, her coworkers heard this and had mortified expressions of disbelief on their faces. To which, the associate nonchalantly said, 'They understand.' No, ma'am -- you don't understand the retail industry is suffering and you're driving nails into its coffin. Macy's Western division cut 1,400 jobs; some of those employees had worked for the firm for 20+ years. Every time a person spends money in a store, s/he chooses to reward the store & its employees with revenue. Treat your clients badly, and you can & will be penalized with no sales.

The prices are about average ($55 - $65 for a women's cut), but considering the quality of the services, it's a steal. In short: run, do not walk, to this salon. You won't regret it.

text: Will Lewis presides as executive chef at this chic seafood-and-steak restaurant. "Seafood-and-steak" may not be totally accurate; the Freight House is somewhat hard to classify due to some real zingers on the menu! The interior is posh and well-kept. There is ample seating for large groups, enough for a wedding reception. Luxurious seats, high ceilings, and flower fans (for circulation up above) were all a nice touch. It could have been more dazzling had there been more lighting. Most of the lights were focused on paintings on the walls (available for purchase). The main dining area was a little dim for my tastes. We had a candle at the table to help us see. For those who prefer a brighter atmosphere, request seating in the rear dining room. There was music but it was difficult to make out through the din of conversation. For a quieter atmosphere, request seating in the rear. There were some unusual appetizers available. We chose calamari and took a risk with the sashimi. The latter was amazingly tasty! We weren't sure if they would get it fantastically wrong or do a stupendous job. The calamari was just right, with a delicious marinara sauce. The calamari was offset with small red and yellow peppers. Sushi, wasabi, and ginger flanked the sashimi. We arrived Friday night without a reservation but luckily we didn't have to wait long. Our waiter was well-informed and hilarious. He was available when needed and checked with us often to see how we were doing many times during the meal. Water, wine, and coffee arrived in a timely manner. His attention to detail was a pleasant surprise -- after bringing coffee that was slightly spilled into the saucer, he offered to bring another cup. We had one or two refills of water then no more attention was paid to us. We requested more and afterwards they came by repeatedly. Our table was cleared efficiently between courses - the wait staff also asked before clearing individual dishes off our table. The seafood mix was pleasantly interesting. the mahi-mahi was prepared well - it was so plentiful, we ended up taking some home. The scallops and shrimp were tender and well-seasoned and went well with the potato. The filet mignon was succulent. The lobster bisque was creamy and arrived piping-hot. Highly recommended! We finished dinner around 10:30 - apparently this restaurant is something of a nightspot in Bucks County. People were dressed to go clubbing! Our check came quickly. Price was slightly above average for a restaurant of that caliber. For four, the total (desserts, drinks, appetizers and entrees) was $150, or $38 a person. Entrees ranged from $16-$30. Appetizers were $8-$12. Credit cards accepted. The Freight House does not disappoint. (Reservations recommended.) Take the train there - it's worth it!

text: The catering service at my wedding was a disaster. In fact, the only positive thing I can say was that the groom and I were too caught up in the excitement and the people to notice many things. What we noticed during our reception included: waiters continuously removing partially full glasses (of water, mixed drinks, wines, etc.) and never bringing water refills, our frustrated and thirsty guests had to go outside to the bar for water -- I should mention we had two handicapped with limited mobility -- coffee and tea were announced to be at the back of the room, no one provided any instructions or assistance for cake cutting and we were surprised to find a plastic layer in the way of the knife, serving sizes were smaller than we were led to believe would be served, and food substitutions were made (i.e. white rice for jasmine and wild rice pilaf), clean up started at least 20min before our reception ended!!! Later I learned, to my extreme embarrassment, that the non-alcoholic strawberry daiquiri mix was simply poured over ice! Glenn specifically asked us to bring a blender to make these; we brought two. My guests were being served strawberry syrup to drink. I also learned that alcoholic beverages were readily being served to teenagers, one of whom was sick in the bathroom. The list continues; but suffice it to say that bartender was a disgrace. I had thought the appetizer spread looked low when I arrived after pictures, but assumed my guests had eaten well. I was mistaken. We had given the children at out wedding cameras for a photo scavenger hunt; though not our intent, their pictures provide excellent evidence of what I (luckily) missed seeing during my wedding. Not only was water removed from the tables while people were still using the glasses, one guest had her half eaten cake removed while turned around talking! She was still in her seat with the cake at her place, but her back was turned. The staff were so difficult to work with that my family setup the rental chairs instead. Moreover, since Culinary Design had another event the next day at our location, they were going to leave the chairs outside, exposed to the elements; my mother, the mother of the bride, went out and folded the chairs in the dark in her gown after guests left to return to a locked building 35min before cleanup was supposed to end! However, the Culinary Design staff was gracious enough to take down our unity candle table, including confiscating the table linen which did not belong to them. They also took our table which we had used as a gift table, which we also had to setup ourselves because Glenn asked us to. We ordered the nearly $500 dessert spread, which the children and professional photographer photographed. As indicated by the wrapping and packaging, the additional cakes were from local super markets! As if that was not enough of an insult, they left the wrapping on and did not provide sufficient serving utensils, etc. Finally, those super-market cakes were put out on our favor table before guests started leaving. The groom and I had personally baked 80 mini-loafs of bread for our guests to take home because we wanted to give them something personal as a thank you for attending and their support over the years. It was an insult to have super-market baked goods, wrapped up right next to our special breads. I am disgusted that Culinary Design Associates would stand behind the service that they provided at our wedding. We had received positive reviews about them and tasted Glenn's samples, which were very good. He seemed to care a lot about his food, and did not come off as a "sales man." We had a lot of confidence in him after our first meeting. However, I should have reconsidered when I had doubts and started feeling uncomfortable communicating with Glenn. He sent rude email responses a couple times. Instead of being able to discuss options and the event with him, we were forced to search the internet (for example, for the cake). I do not think we bothered him too much, especially since we were planning from across the country. I tried to collect several topics for each email so that we contacted him less than a dozen times; but he started to seem quite bothered, and even implied he was too busy because he had more events than usual for August. My advice would be 1) avoid Culinary Design Associates and 2) for whichever caterer you choose, trust your instincts and do not be afraid to switch caterers, and 3) perhaps, sticking to your guns and having more of a presence when uncomfortable with a caterer is better, instead of backing off and trying to accommodate him.

They have an extensive menu covering both breakfast and lunch, and a few daily specials. My meal of choice, half a veggie omelet with hash brows and a biscuit for $5.99. I could go into detail about the omelet and taters, but in the case of Hungry Fox eggs are eggs and hash browns are just what you'd expect, plain and simple. So why four stars? Two words...CHERRY PIE. I'm not talking your average cherry pie with that bizarre filling that you can buy in the baking aisle at Safeway. No, no. I'm talking fresh cherries packed into homemade pastry dough rolled that morning, baked golden brown and served warm. And the best part, if you aren't feeling hungry enough for a slice (yeah, right!) you can order a sliver (half the size of a slice) for a buck!!! I also have a good friend that works there, a waitress named Pam. She used to own my favorite breakfast spot in Tucson, Silver Lining, but had to shut her doors due to the failing economy. I guess taking a seat at Hungry Fox is my way of getting back a piece of breakfast history, and it helps me keep in touch with Pam. text: Every once in a while, as a former big-city dweller, I get a craving for cheap, greasy Chinese take-out. You know -- big battered nuggets of chicken in unidentifiable pink syrup, pan-fried dumplings, and mysteriously salty egg rolls. Maybe I'm alone in this, I don't know. Anyhow, though, my one experience with New Golden Buffet has convinced me that this is not the place to satisfy those cravings. For about thirty bucks, I got a take-out meal consisting of Moo Shu Vegetables, a slightly spicy dish called Ma Pu Tofu, General Tso's Chicken, along with dumplings, pork fried rice, and an egg roll. The dumplings were fine, and the Moo Shu vegetables weren't too bad, but everything else was, frankly, terrible, and as you can see from my other reviews, my standards aren't exactly high. The chicken was almost too hard to chew; the egg roll tasted like it hadn't been completely defrosted before they heated it up, and the tofu dish consisted only of chunks of mushy, flavorless tofu floating in copious amounts of gloppy "sauce" (which appeared to be soy sauce thickened with cornstarch, plus sweetener and hot sauce). The dumplings tasted identical to the dumplings I've eaten in hole-in-the-wall Chinese take-outs around the United States, so they were fine. The Moo Shu vegetables were reasonably good; they tasted fresh, and the flavorings weren't too salty or sweet. Now, most folks go there for the buffet, and there was a bit of a crowd there, so maybe the buffet offerings are better. But for thirty bucks I expected something a little better than this. To top it off, the service was incredibly slow. I'm still looking for that cheap Chinese fix. Website (which features a take-out menu, as well as -- oddly enough -- a list of current quotes from financial markets): http://newgoldenbuffet.com
label: NEG

text: 5 stars for the food, the environment, and the thoughtful service. It's a quaint country farmhouse converted to a wonderful, romantic restaurant, with tables spread throughout its many rooms, most of which have only a few tables providing an intimate, classic dining experience. The food is uniformly fantastic, from the classic Caesar salad prepared tableside, to the big, rich Maryland crab cakes wholly comprised of fresh crab meat and plated across a pair of spicy and pesto sauces. Lobster crepes (stuffed with equally massive amounts of lobster), truly rich lobster bisque, moist tender rack of lamb, and obscenely intense veal tenderloin with exotic mushroom sauce (a special) were equally brilliant examples. My only observation and minor nit about the food was that the meat was not precisely cooked - all the smaller medium-rare items were solidly medium, while the larger filet mignon, ordered medium, came out medium-rare. But all were delectable, and very tender. Desserts were equally brilliant, from the Belgian dark chocolate mousse to the Austrian cheese strudel. The wine list is reasonably large and well selected, especially considering the location, though the markup is enormous. Unfortunately, due to the exorbitant licensing fees charged by Pennsylvania, this is more or less unavoidable, and with a careful search (and sufficient knowledge) reasonable value items can be found. Service was friendly, helpful, and knowledgeable (though the average wine knowledge of the servers isn't large). If you're looking for a fantastic meal in an out-of-the-way, rusticly romantic environment, look no further. They also have a B&B with quite reasonably priced rooms on site.

text: My friend suggested going to Boualong last night, as she raves this is the best Thai restaurant in town, and the only one she goes to. And my friend knows her food! We got there around 7pm, and all six tables were taken already. There was a waiting line in progress, and the waitress told us it was going to be a half hour wait. Seeing as we weren't starving yet, we decided to wait it out. The waiting game takes place in a long and narrow corridor at the back of the restaurant. The restaurant is family-owned, and it's a very old and small building. But somehow the cracks in the walls and the cramped space adds to its charm. There are paintings, photographs, and wooden carvings hanging on the walls for decor. You feel like it's one of those delicious secrets only you know about, except it's one of Edmonton's most popular restaurants. The packed tables and the constant queue attest to that. We didn't have to wait a full half hour for a table. There are two waitresses, and they both work together to serve all tables. I ordered the hot tea, as yesterday was our first day of snow I believe, and I was freezing! It took awhile for the tea to arrive, and I started to wonder if they had forgotten about it, but it came eventually. The food was brought out in a matter of no time, which was very impressive, as there is only a single cook in the kitchen. We ordered the yum and matsamun curry to share between the three of us. The yum was exactly that -- yummy! It's basically glass noodles heaped with peanut sauce, cilantro and mint, carrots, shrimp and chicken. You can order it in different varieties as well. The matsamun curry was very spicy, I was able to tell from the first bite. This is not mild curry they use here, so if you're not used to spicy foods, you might want to ask them which is more mild. I think I'm average when it comes to eating spicy, but I downed two glasses of water with my first helping of the matsamun that night. Despite that, it was delicious. It had chunks of chicken with lots of potatoes, and served with a dish of rice. Our meal came out to be quite inexpensive, at $11 for each of us, including tip. I'll probably come here again, but now I know not to underestimate their curry. And to come before 6pm, so I can get an empty table.

Everything was wonderful and while the ingredient might sound like odd combinations for a burger, they all melded together very well. Scotty's Lakehouse is definitely worth a look - they have a great drink menu and advertised bands starting at 9pm on weekend nights. text: This is a fish out of water story. So I'm en route to El Fuego for some 'ritos when the signage outside Chops catches my roommate's eye. The exchange goes something like this: "I wonder if that place is any good." "I dunno, but it's probably pretty fancy." "Nah dude, check it, $6 burgers!" "Hell, alright, let's go." So we enter, the both of us dressed for dinner at a low-rent burrito spot; t-shirts, shorts, baseball caps. As we cross the threshold of the second set of doors, it's quickly become apparent my initial instinct of "fancy" is about seven shades of understatement. This place is opulent! Before we're able to realize just what we've gotten ourselves into, the greeter (in appropriate suit & tie) approaches and has the same deer-in-headlights look in his eye that I'm sure the both of us maintained. I'm waiting for a line about dress codes and a quick escort to the door we'd just walked through, but was instead welcomed and simply asked, "Two?" Not one to shy away from an awkward social situation for the sake of a decent story, we follow the gentleman to our table located a few feet away. We're seated and finally have a moment to take in just how posh this joint really is. It felt like we had just sat down to dinner in an opera house--incredibly high ceiling, gigantic mural against the far wall, flowing curtains to cover the multi-story windows. I at least have the insight to take off my hat. My roommate does the same. Moments later we're approached by our waitress, Kanika, and are offered our choice of bottled or ice water. With a glance at our matted hair and my college football t-shirt, there's a subtle moment between the three of us and mutual recognition that we don't really belong there. Far from giving us any grief, I detect a slight smile creep onto our server's face and a good-humored acceptance of the situation. Resigned to fully experiencing Chops, we don't even bother looking for any $6 burgers (though I suspect we may have just missed that lunch special and were now considered dinner guests). I order a steak, my dining companion, the veal. A few of the other reviews here have commented on over/under cooked meat, I'll say that Kanika came by our table about 15 minutes after we had put in our order to reassure me that due to the size of my steak, they were making extra sure that it was cooked as ordered--medium. When she returns to our table with our food, I'm faced with what can only be described as an XXL concussion grenade looking slab of meat. This thing is massive. And curiously rotund. I can also say, quite delicious! My roommate enjoys his veal. You know that you're underdressed for an establishment when the team of not one but two people who come by to refold the napkin your company has tossed aside while heading to the restroom are both dressed far nicer than you. All of the desserts shown to us looked incredible but we were both far too stuffed to attempt such a feat. We are presented with the bill, wished a good evening, and asked to come back. Dinner didn't go at all as planned but we had an unexpectedly humorous time and some tasty food. I'll be sure to at least wear pants next time.

text: I was visiting a friend that lives in Boise and she had been wanting to try Boise Fry Company since it opened. She had heard good things and from the reviews here, it seemed like an easy choice for lunch. The register guy was friendly, but a little over zealous. He asked if we had any questions and when we told him we didn't, he then went on to explain how the very self-explanatory menu works. Thanks for the clarity. The burger itself was very good, nearly perfect. I had ordered medium instead of medium well, but it came out to be what I'd consider medium well, anyway. Not sure why a place with quality beef would default to medium-well, but that might be a regional preference. No big deal. Good seasoning, good bread, and among the better burgers I've had. The fries were mediocre. Sad for a place with fry in the name. The Bourgeois fries were a giant let down. For $8 in Boise, you'd expect something impressive. They're fried in duck fat and sprinkled with truffle salt. We didn't taste any distinct duck flavor, just grease. The truffle salt gets old fast. The sweet potato fries were also just greasy and nothing remotely interesting, worse than what I get in L.A.. I really liked the idea of the various salts (I am a salt fiend, anyone that knows me can attest to my love of salt) and the variety of dipping sauces. Sadly, the only dipping sauce that was worthwhile was the spicy fry sauce. The blueberry ketchup is revolting. The sour thai tastes like sour cream, there was nothing "Thai" about it. The Chipotle was fine, but too smokey for my liking. The garlic didn't even smell like garlic, let alone taste like it. I hate smelling like food and we both reeked of oil after we had left. Better ventilation would be ideal. All the doors were open, but it there was still too much oil in the air. My friend and I left feeling overly salted, greased up, and smelling like a fry cook. If I ever went back, I'd get a burger and whatever basic fries to go. Skip the novelty items, they're just not worth it.

text: Let me just say right off the bat that I really like breakfast food - eggs made any number of ways, light, fluffy pancakes, bacon, stuffed french toast... love it all! I have biked by this restaurant many times and did notice the nice breakfast smells emanating from the place but always a little skeptical of a restaurant that looks worn-down from the outside. But I finally stopped by last Saturday morning and had some breakfast. It was surprisingly okay. I had the omelet and my friend had the french toast and they both were pretty decent. We also had the grapefruit juice (pretty fresh and not too sweet) and coffee (kind of watered down but free refills). For me, the portion size was pretty big and they have outdoor seating which was nice since were were able to prop up our bikes on the side and keep an eye on them while we were eating and no one minded that we were dressed in our biking jerseys and covered with road grime. So why four stars? Well, I would give it 3.5 stars if possible but to me, I am really leery of a place where the silverware doesn't look that clean. A couple of things were a little disconcerting - the flying insects that were around (yes, I do realize I was eating outside but when I was ordering inside, still!). Overall, the place didn't scream "clean" at me but I guess that could be part of the rustic ambiance :) Lastly, the potatoes that came with my omelet was a little burnt but I'm not a fan of empty-carb sucking side dishes anyways! There are more breakfast foods on the menu and i will have to come back and try some other dishes but i did take a stroll around and unobtrusively looked at other people's meals that they looked pretty good. The place is pretty packed every Saturday morning I ride by so they must be doing something right! I haven't tried this place for non-breakfast food so I will have to come back and check it out. I am a fan of bacon so the Sonoran-hot dog may be enough to get me to come back.

text: You'd expect a Jewish deli to be able to make the perfect smoked-salmon bagel sandwich. So I went there with high expectations. Although I'm not Jewish, my favorite breakfast meal is smoked salmon on a bagel with cream cheese and onion. I usually make my own at home, with ingredients from Whole Foods. In the '90s, though, I lived near the original Famous 4th Street Deli, so I'd occasionally have the sandwich there. I now live near the new Famous on 19th Street, so I thought I'd try them out this morning. So I ordered the nova version of the bagel sandwich (lox is also available), and headed to Rittenhouse Square to sit on a bench and eat it. What a disappointment. The main problem was that the nova did not seem to be fresh. It had a strange taste -- not a fishy taste, but rather a slightly "sewery" taste. Now, it's assumed that this morning's batch of nova was simply on its last legs, and as soon as this batch is finished, the deli will have a fresh batch of nova to work with, and therefore the problem should not be there in the future. However, the fact that this particular batch would continue to be used beyond its apparent "sell-by" date indicates that there is a deeper problem here. The products need to be monitored more closely for freshness, and when something (especially something as highly perishable as fish) doesn't taste or smell right anymore, it should be disposed of, not served to customers. Beyond that, though, whoever made the sandwich just didn't take enough care to put it together properly. There was a big hunk of cream cheese in the center, without much on the edges of the bagel. It was as if the maker was too lazy to spread the cheese evenly around the whole bagel. It was also a somewhat odd choice to use red onion rather than white or Vidalia (the latter being my favorite on a smoked-salmon bagel). I think of red onion being more a salad onion, not a sandwich onion. The bagel itself was good, so no complaints there. And the slice of tomato was fresh. One pet peeve, though -- why do some places insist on slicing a bagel sandwich in half? Slicing a bagel sandwich does not make it easier to handle (as it does with a hoagie-type sandwich), it makes it more unwieldy, with the contents of the sandwich more apt to fall out. So please, at least ask before slicing. I give two stars rather than one because: 1) The place is pretty and clean and pleasant inside; 2) The wait-staff is attentive and friendly; 3) I want to give them the benefit of the doubt that this was just an anomaly and was simply my bad luck that I got something yucky on my first visit. I'm not sure, though, that I would give them a second visit, so I'll probably never know.

text: For all of us, "in the Biz", we know that getting drunk in the establishment where we work is usually forbidden. Even in the few places that allow such a practice, we veterans know, its just not a good idea. We veterans also know that after certain shifts, getting drunk is an absolute neccesity and there is always a reliable place nearby to do it. Ive worked in the Paoli area for years, at a few different establishments, and for myself and my collegues, its always been TJ's. TJ's is basically a good sports bar with good food and great beer, and it doesnt try to be anything else. Ive tried many of the beers here( awesome) but havent tried much food . Usually Im quite drunk here, so food would be an even bigger mistake. I have tried the wings which were exeptional and a few sandwhiches that I enjoyed ( dont ask me what sandies, the fact that I remember that I liked them should be enough.) Theres alot to do here. Multiple TVs, jukebox, video games, poker tournaments, Fantasy football leagues, quizzo, the list goes on. We often came here for Monday Night Football to cheer our fantasy players (or the Eagles) on. There was a real sense of loss when football season was over, until someone got the great idea to play a DVD on the TVs. From then on, Mondays became movie night. I would argue that you really havent seen Anchorman until youve seen it drunk in a bar with other drunks. I havent been here for a while and cant say if they still do this. It lent itself to criticizm by the few who didnt want to see Will Ferrell naked at a bar. We( like an uglier version of Friends) always tried to get the comfy sofa but its a coveted spot. One thing I love love love about TJs is their takeout beer. They have single bottles of eccentric beers from all round the world. Each cooler is priced the same for example one cooler says " 6pack from this cooler is $14" so you can mix and match with beers from the same cooler. Ive done this and given a 6pack to people as gifts and its always gone over real well. Most shifts at the restraunts ive worked in always started with the phrase, " Did you hear what happened at TJs last night." and whether it be, "who hooked up with who" or "who fought with who" or "did anyone see how drunk and stupid Jim got" ,we would all laugh and laugh ...until we stopped. Thanks TJ!

text: I was the first person to review Tower Tacos. I feel like it is one of my babies, so it makes me sad to see it's decline. Aesthetically, the place has improved via ownership changes, but the food has seriously declined. The owner, Frank has contacted me via Yelp several times. I don't mind being contacted by an owner to ask people to try again or thank them for their review, but in his case, I find his contacts to be pesty and defensive. Still, I wanted to give him the benefit of the doubt. I have tried to revisit Tower Tacos several times, in hopes of changing my mind. I tend to give privately owned establishments a little leeway because I know they don't have corporate gurus directing them and they usually put a little more love into the food. Unfortunately, the food is not the same. They serve Mexican food with new ingredients that are of poor quality. I don't know what else to say. Feel free to read my last review for some explanation. A little over a week ago, I placed a carry out order of tacos and a side of guacamole. The tacos were the El pastor. You usually can't go wrong with El pastor. It's seasoned pork sauteed with chorizo and pineapple on a soft corn tortilla with red onion and cilantro (usually). Any taqueria on Cherokee will do this taco well. Unfortunately, not Tower Tacos. I don't understand... they used to make these great!! I don't know what the meat was seasoned with and white onion? This is not an eastern European restaurant... That onion completely overpowered any sweetness or flavor that the taco could have had. $23 later and no chips were placed in the bag to go with our guacamole and meal. Twer Tacos needs to get back to the basics. Lose the Russian food, unless you are opening a "Tower Stuffed Peppers" restaurant and focus on good, solid Mexican food with fresh, quality ingredients. This is a street where solid Mexican food exists elsewhere.

She approached us to take our drink order before I could even slip into the booth and take off my coat, I was caught off guard and asked what they had available, she pointed to the good ol' soda standard selection. It wasn't until I had already ordered my meal that I found out that I could have created my own flavored egg-cream soda pop, so I was immediately resentful at my plain Coca Cola. text: I hope the other 5 star reviews are joking, sarcastic, or lying, because this restaurant is a stinker. My policy on yelp is to try a restaurant at LEAST twice on different days of the week, before review. Well, now that I've done that, I amhappy to say that I can post this review without having to suffer through Yen Ching's lackluster service, and bile curdling food. Twice, the food arrived in less than 5 minutes. Normally, this is good, but in this case, lukewarm food that has been sitting around for who knows how long does not make a stomach happy. In fact, right across the street is a cafeteria with fast food. Heck, the Hibachi San in the Galleria spends more time cooking your food, and to better results. The food itself is usually flavored strangely. What you get is food that can't compensate for a lack of flavor, and the meaty taste of MSG flakes (a standard flavor additive with Chinese food, and tastes great if used with sanity). Even if you can stomach the food, you will be slammed by one of two types of servers. The nice, but bumbling and inefficient kind, or the mean spirited, but efficient kind. Include the unavailability of parking, the poorly maintained interior, the awards from decades ago, and the lack of authenticity (pineapple chicken? Pineapples are not an indigenous Chinese fruit), and you've found the perfect reason to eat at home (or make the short hop to Mandarin House, on Page). Bottom line: do not eat at Yen Ching's.

text: Let me preface this by saying I was dragged to this place after a 10 hour sales meeting in a hot and steamy conference room. I was starving--and in need of several adult beverages. As this place was described to me I had imagined I'd be embarking on a historical and cultural culinary adventure back through time. You know--chunky bar maids dressed in corseted dresses that functioned for centuries as silicon enhancements holding 8 lead pints in each hand, rogues in the corner laughing and fighting, massive boars heads served on mountainous piles of meat, bards telling their tales of old. And I guess in some demented way this place was just like that....only without the embellishment. Instead of the boar's head we got a small handful of roast beef placed lovingly on a plain bun that was, in turn, placed lovingly on a paper plate of the same size (are we at white castle?). Those Rubenesque hostesses I was imagining turned out to be a friendly--if not forgetful--unceremonious woman who could carry not 8, but 1 pint in each hand. But we did get our Bard. Instead of striking tales of dragons and knights, Mr. J. Alfred Prufrock relinquished a long, tiresome soliloquy on the struggles, tragedies and triumphs that you would expect from a lifetime devoted to being a basketball referee. Now I understand the difference between being captivated with times of yore and being held captive by them.

text: Every time I walk by the Piazza at Schmidt's, I point at Darling's and say "I will never eat there." And then my boyfriend and I usually talk about how unacceptable our attempt at brunch on Memorial Day was. I think several other reviewers have brought up Memorial Day weekend, but I still can't get over it. A group of four of us arrived at Darling's at prime brunch-eating time. There were maybe eight to ten people seated in the restaurant and it was absolutely dead. We walked in and were told that the kitchen was "backed up" and no one in the restaurant had any idea how long it would be. Their excuse was that they had just opened and weren't expecting anyone. I sympathize with a new business, but to not anticipate anyone coming to a restaurant on the one Monday just about everyone in the city has off is just outrageous. One member of our party, a chef, said "Let me get back there, I'll make my own food." This was a joke, but he probably could have turned out meals for everyone in the place a lot faster. As we were laughing about chancing sitting down, two men got up from a booth by the door and told us we should leave - they had been sitting there for well over an hour and had not seen a crumb! OVER AN HOUR. I will never eat here. Every time I walk by it is dead. It is reportedly over priced. And, anyway, even if the service wasn't notoriously slow, why would I want to eat yuppified diner food when authentic, inexpensive, fast diner food is available all over the metro area.

text: Ew. No. NO. 1904 Beerhouse is located inside of River City Casino. They have a pretty wide variety of food. So obviously you know I don't like this place, since I gave it one star. But because I'm trying to be at least a LITTLE bit nice, I'll start with the positives. The place is beautifully decorated. There's a definite German theme. Even the waitresses are dressed like barmaids. It's actually kind of cool. Our waitress was very sweet. She explained everything on the menu to us to the best of her ability, and she even brought us samples of beer that we weren't sure about. Another plus? They have a LOT of beers on tap. The day I went, they had about thirty beers on tap. So that's pretty awesome. Okay, enough of the positives. Lets get down to business. Since they were out of the Kobe Beef Corn Dogs (at noon?!?! Oookay...) we started out with the Crispy Dungeness Crab Fritters. It was like a beer battered crab cake. It was pretty tasty, and the chipotle tartar sauce that came with it was alright. The side of cole slaw was DISGUSTING, though. It was vinegar based, which I usually like, but something tasted way off about it. It was really sour. For the main entree, I settled with the Big and Cheesy Chicken Sandwich. The menu described it as 'crispy thigh chicken, sweet and spicy onions, extra sharp cheddar cheese, St. Louis style BBQ sauce on an onion roll'. Pretty tasty, right? Well, it sounded appetizing to me. Well, it came out, and it was TERRIBLE. First of all, there were way too many slimy onions on the sandwich. I removed those immediately. What was left was a rectangular block of fried chicken on a bun. Hmm. 'Where's my cheese?', I wondered. I bit into the sandwich, and quickly figured out that the cheese was STUFFED into the chicken. It was the most disgusting thing I've bitten into in quite some time. The cheese just oozed out. And there was way too much of it. Oh, and is 'St. Louis style BBQ sauce' really ketchup? Because that's what it tasted like. Ugh. I could only suffer through two bites of the sandwich before I decided I had had enough. The fries were laughable. They looked like McDonald's fries, and tasted like they had been sitting out for a while. Not hot, not crispy, just blah. My mom ordered the pizza, and it was not bad. It tasted like the kind you can get frozen from the grocery store, but whatever. She seemed to like it okay. My sister ordered the basket of fried chicken, which might have been palatable had it not come with three pieces of thigh meat. Maybe something like that should have been mentioned in the menu. She sent that back and went with the ribs, which were decent. Would I come back here? No. Not in a million years. It just wasn't very good, and even though our waitress was nice, it didn't make up for the unbearably slow service.
label: NEG

text: We decided to try this place out last night. I was very pleased with the service, all of the servers were very polite and the owner actually walked around and spoke to the customers after their meals. It is a small hole-in-the-wall restaurant in a very nice area of Nashville. The inside is classy, yet relaxed and informal. We spent around $70 incl. tip for dinner. We decided on the combo dinner for two, it runs about $35. We also ordered two kingfisher beers at 7 bucks a piece, I recommend their Indian wine. I can't remember the name of it but it was smooth, not too sweet and not too dry. A little pricey at $8 a glass, but it complimented the meal wonderfully. The combo came with a starter of pumpkin (?) soup, very flavorful. The main meal included chicken tikka, tandoori chicken, and a ground lamb type of kabob meat. The chicken was great, the lamb was interesting. The taste of the lamb took some getting used to, it was prepared a bit like meatloaf with fresh cilantro and mint leaves. The tandoori chicken was delish of course. We ordered medium spicy, for the curries and that was pretty hot so beware of ordering too spicy here I was breaking a sweat, and I am definitely a Thai food regular. They veggie curry was great, they used fresh and crunchy ingredients which was greatly appreciated! I like my curry to have some texture. It was a bit cheesy, and a little hard to stomach but if you can handle the cream go for it. We also had some type of lamb curry, the cuts of lamb were spot-on. The meat was very tender and there were no scraps (i.e. fat/gristle). The naan was also delish, a bit crispy but still very buttery and tasty. We also ordered the raita (yogurt with cucumber) very good, but I usually like it a bit runny and theirs was very thick. For desert we ordered kheer, the sweet basmati rice pudding. I really liked the presentation with a little cinamon sprinkled on top along with some sliced almonds and a few raisins. Gorgeous. In all we were very happy with this place, next time we will be trying the lunch buffet, at $8.95 per person it should be a great deal considering the quality of food that is served here!
label: POS

text: Absolute hidden gem! This restaurant is in a lttle yellow house on the edge of an industrial area of Antioch Pike north of Harding. It's tucked away on the left two or three buildings up from the motel - it's easy to miss. I've driven by it for almost two years every time we went to lunch at Siam Cafe and I always wondered about it because of the location and it never looked busy. But today I discovered the trick, there is parking around back and that seems to be where everyone parks. Inside is clean and neat with a gallery of photos by a local photographer for your enjoyment or purchase. There is a deck out back but I did not venture out to investigate it this trip. First let me say this place was neat and clean - they scored a perfect 100 on their Metro Health Inspection! The owners are very friendly. I talked with them to get their story. He has been baking since he was in his teens and in fact, his bakery back in Bosnia is still going strong. They moved here 10 years ago and like most people from that region, they always tell you how appreciative they are for this country and the opportunities they have had here. I wasn't sure what I wanted to try first. She had a Chevapi plate that she had prepared in the past for another customer that she thought I might like it - it was fiveor six pieces of chevapi with a sauce on top of vegetables and rice with a piece of homemade pita bread. I also couldn't resist the cheese filled burak as I have had a Russian dish that was similar at Taste of Russia and miss it now that they are closed. She brought the burek out first along with ShangriLa tea - I had it somewhere the other day but don't remember it being this good. I only ate about a third wanting to save room for my chevapi plate. It is wonderful. The cheese is rolled up in a sort of phyllo or layered dough and then baked. The outside is crispy, the inside dough chewy and the cheese wonderful. Next came the chevapi plate. Chevapi is a minced meat/sausage like food from Bosnia. Everything on the plate ws wonderful including the homemade pita that is a cross between the traditional pocket pita and the more breadlike pocketless pita. Knowing that he was a baker, I had to try the baklava and it was some of the best I have had without a doubt and it was a nice large serving (almost too much considering how rich baklava is) and fresh. And to balance it out, I had a cup of Turkish coffee that was a perfect way to balance out the richness of the baklava. This is so close to work that I will be a regular here. text: Chifa was on the top of my list for Center City Sips. I absolutely love Sips because it's a great way to get an introduction to a restaurant without committing to spending a bunch of money. BUT at Chifa, I was denied the Sips experience. If I can say one thing about the service and general feel of this place it's MILITANT. As soon as I walked in, I got a spiel - "Sips is ONLY downstairs." In the basement. Where there's not nearly enough seating for everyone. The UPSTAIRS, mind you, is almost completely empty at 5:00 and I would think a newish restaurant could benefit from looking crowded upstairs where people outside can see. When my friends arrived, there was no seating and virtually nowhere to stand, so we decided to head upstairs and eat like civilized people with a table and space and service. The bartender gave us a hard time about ordering sips drinks and taking them upstairs. Lame. We go upstairs and ask for a table. The server says the table is only for the full menu - we accept these terms. At this point one friend has wandered off to make a phone call and the waitress says "You do have 3 people right." 3 seconds later "Where is your third person, does he know where you'll be." These servers need to CHILL! Finally, they take their food way too seriously. The server's description of the menu was right on, but quite a few times things were over explained. Honestly, though, I don't think it's the server's fault. It's the food's fault. One of the things we ordered was the Anticuchos. It was delicious, but the skewers basically came with 6 (yes, six) sauces - 3 on the side and 3 already on the meat. And it was about 12 pieces of meat total. That's totally overwhelming for any palate. Fun, but kind of pointless. The night was a blur of sauces and tastes and nothing particularly stood out accept the chimichurri. It was just too much on every dish. Also, when I order fries, I expect there to be a bunch, not just a handful. The rest of the night, we basically had to shoo the servers from taking our dishes prematurely and then we had the banana-pumpkin funnel cake. Sorry, but this dessert looked like a turd. I KNOW there have got to be classier ways to plate funnel cake. And it was greasy, not crispy. Definitely not worth $8. Finally, I can say I won't be going back here because I feel tricked. I wanted Sips, damn it. The restaurant knew that if people really wanted to stay, they would head upstairs and spend more money. But they could have just been nice about it and opened Sips to the whole restaurant. The people would have left by 7 or so anyway! Instead they made the Sips patrons feel lowly and acted really full of themselves. The upstairs really wasn't THAT special. At a restaurant, you don't get to treat your guests differently depending on what they order (especially when you are OFFERING things at a discount). I think Chifa could benefit from a slice of humble pie.

It revealed itself as what it really is: a big indifferent wildly overpriced cafeteria. I had three cuts of steak, and they were the fattiest pieces of meat I've ever encountered in a restaurant. Ghastly pieces of glistening gristle. I shrugged off the first piece -- shit happens -- but it was nasty. The second piece, however, was equally yellow and what little meat in it was stringy with fat and muscle. By the third piece,a 2-inch square of "garlic-flavored sirloin" -- gristle rolled in burnt garlic (blech!) --my stomach was beginning to roil as I gazed at the mounting plate of picked-apart blubber. My dinner companion thought I had to be exaggerating. He forked a piece of the "meat" from my plate and popped it into his mouth, at which point he got a funny sick look on his face for there he sat, his mouth full of nasty rubbery fat. He had a decision to make: eat his words or eat a big chunk of cellulite. Even though he hates to be wrong, and will eat nearly anything, he spit the fat out: it was that disgusting. My last attempt was a bit of parmesan-crusted pork tenderloin, which was dry but tasty and, praise be, trimmed of fat. However, by then my appetite and my patience were shot. All I could think of was that this festival of fat was going to cost me $50 plus $10 for a glass of cheap wine. And tip. All that for a tricked-out cafeteria. When the waiter brought the check I pointed to all the fat on my plate. He responded like a cafeteria clerk, noting in a flat voice that "some cuts of meat are fatty." Of course! That's why we trim them, pal, before charging people $50 for pieces of low-grade sirloin. Pony up for a ginsu knife and some quality control, Fatty de Chao! And for you carnivores: save your money and go to a cheap steakhouse, where the meat and the check won't make you sick to your stomach.

text: Great barbecue isn't easy to find in Tucson, and no real barbecue tradition (much less barbecue culture) has developed here. Brushfire BBQ, taking advantage of this cultural void, serves up barbecue from a variety of American traditions, offering most types of meat most commonly barbecued around the country - brisket, ribs, pork shoulder, chicken, and sausage. In addition, they're offering smoked-then-fried chicken wings, a relatively new and relatively rare entry into the barbecue arena. In addition, Brushfire offers a variety of sides, ranging from the traditional (corn on the cob, three varieties of coleslaw, and baked beans), to something more unusual ("Messy Fries," french fries topped with barbecued meat, sauce, and cheese). I was there for lunch, and tried the brisket sandwich with hot sauce, and the vinegar coleslaw. The sandwich was served simply on a toasted roll loaded with slices of brisket doused with sauce. The brisket was nicely done, tender, and showing a nice pink smoke ring near the meat's surface. The sauce was slightly sweet, pleasantly hot without being at all overpowering (if I had wanted to be overpowered, however, there was a large selection of hot sauces on a shelf with which I could have doctored up my sandwich nicely). The slaw, tart and a little sweet, was fresh, crisp, and crunchy. I also had an order of the messy fries, topped with pork, Brushfire's Balsamic Bacon sauce (very good) and some shredded provolone cheese. The fries seem to be batter-dipped prior to frying, and are quite crisp and delicious. The barbecue topping turns them into an over-the-top appetizer or side. The service is excellent - place your order at the counter and a server will bring it to your table when it's ready, which won't be long. The previously mentioned hot sauce bar is available at any time, and the tables are supplied with extra Brushfire Mild and Hot BBQ sauces, plenty of napkins, toothpicks, and wet-naps for your wiping pleasure. Prices are on the high end of the fastfood range, but are more than reasonable considering what you get. For the regular sandwich, slaw, messy fries, and a large soft drink, the cost was around 12 bucks. Parking is a bit of a pain, as the restaurant is right on a busy stretch of Campbell Ave with only a few parking spots right off the street, but it's hard to imagine how they could improve that. The downside is that the menu simply lists all the beers and the only categorization offered is by country. So, if you are not an expert in beers or haven't done your research before going, you might not know what to order. The menu should include descriptions of the beers, or at the very least, the servers should be experts and know what to recommend. We wanted to try new and different beers, but weren't that happy with what we chose because of the lack of guidance. If you know what kind of beers you want to try before you go, then Shallos is a good choice. Do your research - the website lists them. The food was not good at all. Unlike the beer list, the dinner menu didn't have much to choose from. I decided to order the Filet Mignon, but should have known better based on the price ($14?!). It was bland and overcooked. text: Whenever I move to a new area, job one (realistically job twenty or so, but that's not effective rhetoric) is hunting down a good place to pick up used vinyl. BWS eluded me for a few months, but upon discovering it I have fallen in love. Granted our courtship has been fast and capricious, as things tend to be at the beginning, but I imagine my feelings won't be changing any time soon. Not only does Beautiful World offer a considerably wider inventory than its closest analog in the area (the misleadingly titled Marvelous), loads of new material is constantly spilling in, and the staff are quite knowledgeable and are not pretentious, self-styled music elitists, a common shortcoming at such establishments. They also endorse reuse of the plastic bags they supply, which I like. Many may find the simple alphabetical organization under genre headings (as opposed to organization by band name) an inconvenience, but I think it only adds to your delight when you stumble unawares across, say, Mott the Hoople's "All the Young Dudes", as I did earlier this week while perusing the M's, rather than noticing a divider with the band's name and flipping right to it. I find the scavenger hunt format to be much more exciting. Some may agree. Beautiful World also has a modest but appreciable amount of new vinyl, both reissues and contemporary stuff, which is often an attractive alternative to CDs or mp3s because many bands these days include with their new releases on vinyl a code and instructions for downloading the entire album for free, if you consider having a digital copy necessary. I'm not really in the market for used CDs anymore, but a cursory survey suggests that their selection in this department is also respectable, if that's your thing. Also, if you come across any Flying Burrito Brothers in your browsing, please purchase it for me and I will reward you handsomely. Too long has that record evaded my best efforts to secure a copy.

Having worked for Aramark catering for years, I'm sure this was frozen food from some food manufacturer. To add insult to injury, when the bill came I was horrified to see that they'd charged $24 for the "lobster" ravioli. Some special!!! This is a heist to overcharge you for pre-made, poor quality food. Olive Garden does better disguising their dishes--Cafe Mulino could take a few lessons from them. text: What a letdown. My wife and I were very excited to try this place. It's a new "rustic Italian" joint in our own neighborhood! Well, unless rustic Italian means stale bread, chewy pasta, high prices, and fatty meat, they really missed the mark. --The Good-- The experience started off on the right foot. The ambiance was very nice. The mix of faux-worn floorboards and crisp light wood tables, combined with the quaint patio dining option, made for a beautiful picture and a pair of optimistic diners. Our server was helpful and mostly prompt. The fried mozzarella was well seasoned and thinly breaded. Very tasty. But, unfortunately, the good news ends there. --The Bad-- First, the menu was out of sorts. There were duplicate pages and even lunch menus mixed in. The waitress also informed us that there were no soups, nor was there any of the Chilean Sea Bass, much to my dismay. The bread and olive oil was another letdown. The bread was very stale and bland. I made the comment to my wife that Wonder Bread would have been more welcome. The oil was not spiced, nor was there any salt and pepper for us to remedy. For the main course, I ordered a steak dish with meat sauce and a side of orzo. The steak was by far the fattiest piece of meat I have ever been served. The orzo was very bland (and remember -- no salt on the table). My wife ordered the spaghetti marinara. How can you screw that up? They found a way. The pasta was mealy and the sauce uninspired. --The Ugly-- To add insult to injury, the check totaled over $40. For this neighborhood, I expected to get away with $15 per person at the most for this low-end fare. I could see if there were alcohol, but it's a BYOB joint and we arrived unprepared. All in all, it probably was not the worst meal I've ever eaten. But it's certainly in the bottom five for the price they charged. I've read some other reviews that rave about this place, and I honestly don't get it. Maybe we hit them on a bad night. But the nature of the negatives we experienced have served to chase us away forever. There are enough other options in the area.
label: NEG

text: This place has been on my radar for a while because: (1) It's in my hood; (2) it's Asian (Japanese street food from Osaka!); and (3) when you order, you get to say "balls" (I'm 5 years old). I was surprised to learn that the balls are not fried, but rather hand-cooked in a waffle-iron like contraption with divets the size of golf balls. And while the skins were slightly crisp, the inside was warm and doughy. For lunch, I ordered the health salad, and the classic takoyaki with shrimp. If you are the kind of person that likes quinoa-like grains, you will LOVE the health salad. It's a blackish grain with some veggies cut up on top (carrots, cukes) served with two vinaigrettes. The green pesto-like dressing was delicious, and the salad kept me full for the rest of the afternoon. Takoyaki balls were ooey-gooey and totally scrumptious - unlike anything I've ever eaten before (note: if you don't like Nori, skip the classic takoyaki flavor). A few weeks later, around dinner time, I had a hankering for these balls (hehe), so dining companion and I ventured over. I got the health salad, AGAIN, and the BBQ takoyaki with shrimp. DC got some yakisoba noodles and the sweet 'n sour miso takoyaki with chicken. I definitely prefer the seafood fillings (shrimp, octopus) to the meat fillings. I also loved the BBQ sauce, but was more or less "meh" on the sweet 'n sour miso. Yakisoba was a little too sweet for my liking...but DAMN those balls are good. This is not an everyday place for me, but I know I will get sharp cravings for these tasty little snacks on a fairly regular basis, which is why Maru Global gets 4 stars.

I'll say thank you b/c I just saved you $50 and a really disappointing dinner.

text: Ambience here is beautiful, the lighting, everything. We started with the kobe sliders (HIGHLY recommend them!), and each had the filet. They bring you a choice of knives and you can pick which one to use to make your dining experience even better. The sides were deeeee liscious. We had the broccolini, and the lyonnaise potatoes. After all the delicious wine and food, I was so stuffed and enjoyed my leisurely walk afterwards around rittenhouse square. Totally perfect location, totally perfect food, totally perfect service....now...the price, however, is for those who make a lot of money. I think I'll only eat here a couple times a year. I highly highly recommend!

text: This was a good time more because of the Yelper company I had rather than the scare factor of the place. But for what it lacked in scare & gore it made up for with hilarious cheese. I would give 5 stars alone for the awesome stash the first "tour guide" was wearing. Other than stumbling face first into plywood walls it was a good time, but still has a lot of room for improvement. Also be prepared to be searched before entering. Safety first kids!
label: POS

text: Dad & I have been here for lunch several times and have enjoyed each of our visits. They serve great food at very reasonable prices. Just recalling the Shrimp Lo Mein makes my mouth water! I'm a big fan of their seaweed salad. It doesn't taste any better than anyplace else, really, but they do such a nice job with presentation. Always something a little different, like on a plate with tomatoes or with planks of cucumber underneath. All the sushi we've tried has been excellent. Good proportion of fillings to rice, and well rolled. Fresh & tasty. Dad's litmus test for Chinese restaurants is their Egg Foo Young, particularly if they have Shrimp. Panda Garden does, and this has to be his favorite Egg Foo Young in the area. Hot, delicious, and full of nice-sized shrimp. We have started getting an extra order to take home. Service has always been fast and friendly, and they consistently keep my soda full. Just a few disappointing things: The last few times we've been there, the fish tank has been gross-looking with cloudy water and sickly fish. If they can't keep it up, please just get rid of it. Not happy that they haven't had hokkigai (surf clam) the last several times we've ordered it. The location of the bathroom (outside!) is very poor.
label: POS

text: This place is so refreshing. The location and shop itself is so quaint and cute. I love the menu with its chalk and blackboard layout. The curried chicken sandwich is the best I have had.
label: POS

text: Sorry to say, but this place is overrated. At least for dinner. From the past reviews, it would seem that brunch is far and away a better option, which I've yet to try. I used to live a stone's throw from this BYOB, and I've had several friends on separate occasions enthuse about the food, prompting me to eat there more than a few times. Each instance has been progressively more underwhelming. Though the decor appears Moroccan in sensibility, Figs doesn't purport to feature exclusively North African cuisine. Still, the menu seems to be confused as to its culinary pedigree: baked brie, tuna sashimi, and gazpacho alongside lamb tagine (the best thing on the menu) and sesame-crusted salmon? Where's the b'stila, or chicken with preserved lemons? My last time there, it took forever to be served water and a little bread w/hummus, and strangely, no one offered to uncork our wine bottle. My eggplant lasagna appetizer was dry and overcooked, and my swordfish main was decent, but only just. Their website claims that the owner M. Rouissiya often cooks, waits tables and chats with the clientele; I've never seen him once in all the times I've been there. (It's rumored he's a bit of a jerk in the way he treats his mostly Latino staff, anyhow.) In my opinion, the prices are not merited, given food this pedestrian. The mint tea's not even complimentary...
label: NEG

text: This restaurant is excellent. i LOVE this place!!! We get the family style dinner and its phenomenal. This family owned restaurant has great service and the best food. Very nice people and they go out of their way to make sure you are satisfied. I love the veal dishes and the spinach tortellini. The ambiance is perfect..very cozy feel..i love the way its decorated with stone walls and a beautiful fireplace. Also, the vegetable bosnian soup is soooooo yummy!!! i can never get tired of eating here! I highly recommend Grbic to everyone.
label: POS

text: Came here after visiting a Black Bear for the first time in Tulare. First off, you need to order the pancakes - just yum! These are the best pancakes I've ever had. For the price, the portions here are humongous. I got the big bear breakfast (swapped the meat for some taters) and it was really filling. I like the kitsch of a log cabin/bear themed diner, the service was friendly and fast, and it was reasonably priced. Can't go wrong with that!
label: POS

text: Service was abyssmal - many tables around us left after no one seemed interested in waiting on customers. Food was passable at best. Portion size was TINY! I would have given them only one star, but the multiple big screen televisions earned them an extra star. Don't come here expecting too much and you MAY not be disappointed.
